The '''62nd Academy Awards''' ceremony, presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best [[1989 in film|films of 1989]] and took place on March 26, 1990, at the [[Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]] in [[Los Angeles]] beginning at 6:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]] / 9:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Eastern Time Zone|EST]]. During the ceremony, AMPAS presented [[Academy Awards]] (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 23 categories. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[Gilbert Cates|Gil Cates]] and directed by [[Jeff Margolis]]. Actor [[Billy Crystal]] hosted the show for the first time.<ref name="lat" /> Three weeks earlier, in a ceremony held at [[The Beverly Hilton]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]] on March 3, the [[Academy Award for Technical Achievement|Academy Awards for Technical Achievement]] were presented by hosts [[Richard Dysart]] and [[Diane Ladd]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Past Scientific & Technical Awards Ceremonies|url=http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|access-date=July 31, 2013|publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140213185729/http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|archive-date=February 13, 2014}}</ref>

''[[Driving Miss Daisy]]'' won four awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Cieply |first=Michael |title='Driving Miss Daisy,' Tandy Win Top Oscars : Academy Awards: Day-Lewis is named best actor. Stone is best director for 'Fourth of July.' |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-03-27-mn-252-story.html |access-date=August 20, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 27, 1990 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140710033836/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-03-27/news/mn-252_1_miss-daisy |archive-date=July 10, 2014 }}</ref> Other winners included ''[[Glory (1989 film)|Glory]]'' with three awards, ''[[Born on the Fourth of July (film)|Born on the Fourth of July]]'', ''[[The Little Mermaid (1989 film)|The Little Mermaid]]'', and ''[[My Left Foot]]'' with two, and ''[[The Abyss]]'', ''[[Balance (1989 film)|Balance]]'', ''[[Batman (1989 film)|Batman]]'', ''[[Cinema Paradiso]]'', ''[[Common Threads: Stories from the Quilt]]'', ''[[Dead Poets Society]]'', ''[[Henry V (1989 film)|Henry V]]'', ''[[Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade]]'', ''[[The Johnstown Flood (1989 film)|The Johnstown Flood]]'', and ''[[Work Experience (film)|Work Experience]]'' with one. The telecast garnered more than 40 million viewers in the United States.

==Winners and nominees==
<!-- Please do not add any fact or statement below unless you have a credible source verifying it. Otherwise, it will be promptly removed. -->

The nominees for the 62nd Academy Awards were announced on February 14, 1990, at the [[Samuel Goldwyn Theater]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], by [[Karl Malden]], president of the academy, and actress [[Geena Davis]].<ref name="PWBV">{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=764}}</ref> ''[[Driving Miss Daisy]]'' received the most nominations with nine total; ''[[Born on the Fourth of July (film)|Born on the Fourth of July]]'' came in second with eight.<ref>{{cite news|title='Miss Daisy' in the Driver's Seat : Movie Is Nominated for 9 Oscars |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-02-14-mn-811-story.html |access-date=August 20, 2013 |date=February 15, 1990 |work=Los Angeles Times |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005011901/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-02-14/news/mn-811_1_driving-miss-daisy |archive-date=October 5, 2013 }}</ref> Winners were announced during the awards ceremony on March 26, 1990.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Winners |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-03-27-ca-357-story.html |access-date=August 20, 2013 |date=March 27, 1990 |work=Los Angeles Times |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005004736/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-03-27/entertainment/ca-357_1_driving-miss-daisy |archive-date=October 5, 2013 }}</ref> ''Driving Miss Daisy'' became the third film to win [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] without a [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]] nomination.<ref>{{cite news|last=Hughes |first=Mark |title=Ten Facts You Should Know About The Oscars |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/markhughes/2013/02/23/ten-facts-you-should-know-about-the-oscars/ |access-date=August 20, 2013 |work=[[Forbes]] |date=February 23, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005002559/http://www.forbes.com/sites/markhughes/2013/02/23/ten-facts-you-should-know-about-the-oscars/ |archive-date=October 5, 2013 }}</ref> At age 80, [[Jessica Tandy]] became the oldest Best Actress winner.<ref>{{harvnb|Osborne|2013|p=423}}</ref> [[Kenneth Branagh]] was the fifth person nominated for Best Lead Actor and Best Director for the same film.<ref name="CWBV">{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=1163}}</ref>

==Ceremony information==
[[File:Billy Crystal VF 2012 Shankbone.JPG|thumb|130px|right|[[Billy Crystal]] hosted the 62nd Academy Awards.|alt=Photo of Billy Crystal.]]

After the negative reception received from the [[61st Academy Awards|preceding year's ceremony]], AMPAS created an Awards Presentation Review Committee to evaluate and determine why the telecast earned such a negative reaction from the media and the entertainment industry.<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=750}}</ref><ref name="SnowJob">{{cite news |last=Hofler |first=Robert |title=Snow Job |url=http://www.lamag.com/features/2010/03/01/snow-job |access-date=September 13, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles (magazine)|Los Angeles]] |date=March 1, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005190927/http://www.lamag.com/features/2010/03/01/snow-job |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> The committee later determined that Carr's biggest mistake was allowing the questionable opening number to run for 12 minutes. Producer and former [[Directors Guild of America]] president [[Gilbert Cates]], who headed the committee, said that Carr would not have received such harsh criticism if the number had been much shorter.<ref name="SnowJob"/> Newly elected AMPAS president [[Karl Malden]] also commented on last year's telecast, "Some of the people in the Academy felt the show got a little out of control."<ref name="Cates"/>

In September 1989, Cates was chosen as producer of the 1990 telecast.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ryan |first=Desmond |title=New Producer Is Chosen To Plan The 1990 Oscar Presentation |url=http://articles.philly.com/1989-09-24/entertainment/26104285_1_oscar-show-allan-carr-gilbert-cates |work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |access-date=August 20, 2013 |date=September 24, 1989 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131022115405/http://articles.philly.com/1989-09-24/entertainment/26104285_1_oscar-show-allan-carr-gilbert-cates |archive-date=October 22, 2013 }}</ref> Malden explained the decision to hire him, saying, "Cates, a veteran film and TV director known for his tasteful work in both media, will attempt to rectify the damage the last Oscar show did to the Academy's reputation."<ref name="Cates" /> The following January, actor and comedian [[Billy Crystal]] was chosen as host of the ceremony.<ref>{{cite news|title=Billy Crystal to be Host of Oscar Ceremonies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/01/02/arts/billy-crystal-to-be-host-of-oscar-ceremonies.html |access-date=August 19, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=January 2, 1990 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131007050530/http://www.nytimes.com/1990/01/02/arts/billy-crystal-to-be-host-of-oscar-ceremonies.html |archive-date=October 7, 2013 }}</ref> "We are extremely pleased to have Billy host the show," Cates said in a press release justifying his choice. "His unique talents and his ability to handle the unexpected will be important assets this year."<ref>{{cite news|title=Billy Crystal Will Host Oscar Ceremonies |url=http://www.deseretnews.com/article/79543/BILLY-CRYSTAL-WILL-HOST-OSCAR-CEREMONIES.html |access-date=January 22, 2014 |work=[[Deseret News]] |date=January 1, 1990 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140710153452/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/79543/BILLY-CRYSTAL-WILL-HOST-OSCAR-CEREMONIES.html |archive-date=July 10, 2014 }}</ref>

Cates christened the show with the theme "Around the World in 3 1/2 Hours," commenting that it would be "a party thrown around the world".<ref name="nyt">{{cite news|title=New Host and New Technology, But a Familiar Oscar Show |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/03/28/movies/review-television-new-host-and-new-technology-but-a-familiar-oscar-show.html |work=The New York Times |date=March 28, 1990 |access-date=March 17, 2010 |first=Janet |last=Maslin |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307005539/http://www.nytimes.com/1990/03/28/movies/review-television-new-host-and-new-technology-but-a-familiar-oscar-show.html |archive-date=March 7, 2016 }}</ref> He also explained, "The world is changing, and hopefully the awards show is changing, matching the changes in the world."<ref name="Cates"/> In tandem with the program's theme, several presenters announced the winners from various international locales such as Buenos Aires, London, Moscow, and Sydney, Australia.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ryan |first=Desmond |title=Moscow To Take Part In The Oscar Ceremony |url=http://articles.philly.com/1990-03-11/entertainment/25904911_1_foreign-language-film-moscow-oscar |access-date=August 20, 2013 |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=March 11, 1990 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131022115339/http://articles.philly.com/1990-03-11/entertainment/25904911_1_foreign-language-film-moscow-oscar |archive-date=October 22, 2013 }}</ref>

Several other people participated in the production of the ceremony. Documentary filmmaker [[Chuck Workman]] assembled a montage saluting "100 Years at the Movies" that was shown at the beginning of the telecast.<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=771}}</ref> Film composer and musician [[Bill Conti]] served as musical director for the ceremony.<ref>{{cite news|title=Composer Conti Will Conduct at 62nd Academy Awards |url=http://www.deseretnews.com/article/83231/COMPOSER-CONTI-WILL-CONDUCT-AT-62ND-ACADEMY-AWARDS.html |access-date=February 2, 2014 |work=Deseret News |date=January 24, 1990 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140710155052/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/83231/COMPOSER-CONTI-WILL-CONDUCT-AT-62ND-ACADEMY-AWARDS.html |archive-date=July 10, 2014 }}</ref> Dancer and singer [[Paula Abdul]] supervised the Best Song nominee performances and a dance number featuring the Best Costume Design nominees.<ref>{{cite news|title=Abdul to Choreograph Academy Awards|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=EWxCAAAAIBAJ&sjid=IasMAAAAIBAJ&pg=3690,516195|access-date=August 17, 2013|newspaper=Middlesboro Daily News|date=January 11, 1990|archive-date=March 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210306105205/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=EWxCAAAAIBAJ&sjid=IasMAAAAIBAJ&pg=3690,516195|url-status=live}}</ref> Singer [[Diana Ross]] performed the Oscar-winning song "[[Over the Rainbow]]" in a tribute to the 50th anniversary of ''[[The Wizard of Oz (1939 film)|The Wizard of Oz]]''.<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=777}}</ref>

===Box office performance of nominees===
At the time of the nominations announcement on February 14, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $244 million with an average of $48.9 million.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars>{{cite news|title=1989 Academy Award Nominations and Winner for Best Picture |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1989&p=.htm |access-date=June 17, 2014 |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140614052144/http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1989&p=.htm |archive-date=June 14, 2014 }}</ref> ''Dead Poets Society'' was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees with $95.8 million in domestic box office receipts. The film was followed by ''Field of Dreams'' ($64.4&nbsp;million), ''Born on the Fourth of July'' ($48.6&nbsp;million), ''Driving Miss Daisy'' ($35.6&nbsp;million) and ''My Left Foot'' ($2.1&nbsp;million).<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/>

Of the 50 grossing movies of the year, 43 nominations went to 14 films on the list. Only ''Parenthood'' (8th), ''Dead Poets Society'' (9th), ''When Harry Met Sally...'' (10th), ''Field of Dreams'' (17th), ''Born on the Fourth of July'' (25th), ''Driving Miss Daisy'' (36th), and ''Sex, Lies, and Videotape'' (45th) were nominated for Best Picture, acting, directing, or screenwriting. The other top 50 box office hits that earned nominations were ''Batman'' (1st), ''Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade'' (2nd), ''Lethal Weapon 2'' (3rd), ''Back to the Future II'' (6th), ''The Little Mermaid'' (12th), ''The Abyss'' (22nd), and ''Black Rain'' (27th).<ref>{{cite news|title=1989 Box Office Grosses (as of February 13, 1990) |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1990-02-12&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1989&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |access-date=February 14, 2014 |work=Box Office Mojo |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140710160813/http://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1990-02-12&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1989&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |archive-date=July 10, 2014 }}</ref>

===Critical reviews===
The show received a mixed reception from media publications. Some media outlets were more critical of the show. Film critic [[Janet Maslin]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' gave an average review of Crystal but lamented, "The effort to make this year's Academy Awards show an international media miracle led to nothing but headaches."<ref name="nyt"/> ''[[The Washington Post]]'' television critic [[Tom Shales]] bemoaned, "while Crystal's opening monologue seemed to hit the right notes, he hit fewer and fewer as the evening wore on; his interjected quips between awards were mostly uninspired." He also criticized the dance numbers and numerous "Around the World" cutaways, calling it pointless.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Shales|first1=Tom|title=On the Air: Billy Crystal And the Night That Wouldn't End|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |page=C1}}</ref> [[Howard Rosenberg]] of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' quipped that the broadcast was "a conventional telecast that was arguably an extension of an industry calcified by convention". He gave positive remarks toward Crystal but felt that "The Oscarcast was an old kid on the block."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rosenberg |first1=Howard |title=TV Review: Another Dose of Business as Usual |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-03-27-ca-361-story.html |access-date=May 7, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 27, 1990 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711015746/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-03-27/entertainment/ca-361_1_big-business |archive-date=July 11, 2014 }}</ref>

Other media outlets received the broadcast more positively. ''[[USA Today]]'' television critic Matt Roush lauded "...the glib and savvy Billy Crystal, who kept things as lively and funny as he could all night long. What a chore, too." He concluded that, "Hollywood no doubt went to bed happy (maybe early), because for a change, Oscar didn't embarrass himself."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Roush|first1=Matt|title=Crystal sparkles on safe and stately show|work=USA Today|page=4D |date=March 27, 1990}}</ref> Mike Drew of the ''[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]]'' remarked, "While too "inside" and not as funny as Hollywood thinks he is, Crystal was an efficient host."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Drew|first1=Mike|title=Oscar show slow, but not bad|work=[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]]|page=4 |date=March 28, 1990}}</ref> Film critic [[Carrie Rickey]] of ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' wrote, "It was encouraging that director Gilbert Cates took the opportunity to emphasize films instead of chorus girls." She also extolled Crystal's performance, acknowledging that his "nimble opening number set a [[Johnny Carson]] comic tone."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rickey |first1=Carrie |title=An Oscar Telecast with Taste |url=http://articles.philly.com/1990-03-28/news/25902145_1_race-relations-first-feature-film-editing |access-date=June 1, 2014 |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=March 28, 1990 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131106051245/http://articles.philly.com/1990-03-28/news/25902145_1_race-relations-first-feature-film-editing |archive-date=November 6, 2013 }}</ref>

===Ratings and reception===
The American telecast on ABC drew in an average of 40.24 million people over its length, which was a 5% decrease from the [[61st Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Johnson |first=Greg |title=Call It the Glamour Bowl |url=https://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |access-date=August 26, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 18, 1999 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928053918/http://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |archive-date=September 28, 2013 }}</ref> An estimated 70 million total viewers watched all or part of the awards.<ref>{{cite news|title=Oscars Push ABC to Win Ratings Race |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-04-03-ca-864-story.html |access-date=June 6, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 3, 1990 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711022630/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-04-03/entertainment/ca-864_1_ratings-race |archive-date=July 11, 2014 }}</ref> The show also drew lower [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony, with 27.82% of households watching over a 49.42 share.<ref>{{cite news|title=ABC gets an Oscar boost|work=USA Today|page=3D |date=April 4, 1990}}</ref>

In July 1990, the ceremony presentation received five nominations at the [[42nd Primetime Emmy Awards|42nd Primetime Emmy]]s.<ref>{{cite news|title=Primetime Emmy Award database |url=http://www.emmys.com/shows/62nd-annual-academy-awards |access-date=April 29, 2014 |publisher=[[Academy of Television Arts and Sciences]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711022927/http://www.emmys.com/shows/62nd-annual-academy-awards |archive-date=July 11, 2014 }}</ref> Two months later, the ceremony won one of those nominations for [[Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Production Design for a Variety or Reality Series|Outstanding Art Direction for a Variety or Music Program]] (Roy Christopher and Greg Richman).<ref>{{cite news|last1=Lipton |first1=Lauren |title='The Simpsons' Named Best Animated Series in Early Awards |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-09-17-ca-663-story.html |access-date=May 21, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711023116/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-09-17/entertainment/ca-663_1_comedy-series/2 |archive-date=July 11, 2014 }}</ref>
